metadata.title: Expected, Observed
metadata.greeting_note: hello lexicon: Hindi, one word (Liam takes the one-word budget). Wagwan check: charsum('claude-liam-expected-vs-observed') = 3162, 3162 % 10 == 2, not 0 — no Wagwan.
metadata.purpose: INFO 7375 Week 1 graded assignment. ONE concept from Chapter 1: expected count (665.24) vs observed count (630) — a sampling gap is not evidence the probabilities are wrong.
metadata.author: Arundhati Kandelkar
metadata.evidence: Every number on screen is printed by lessons/01-randomness-and-first-prompts/code/main.py, unmodified, seed=7, count=1000. Verified 2026-09-26. Derived arithmetic (665.24, 35.24, 5.3%) is recomputed from those printed values, never hand-estimated.
metadata.scope_note: SOFTMAX IS DELIBERATELY ONE BEAT (B02), not a derivation. The assignment's dominant failure mode is covering several concepts badly; the max-subtraction is a SEPARATE listed concept. B02 exists only to source the 0.6652 that B03 multiplies, and says so on screen.
metadata.constructed_disclosure: B05 is the ONLY constructed illustration. Its two numbers (665.24, 630) are real; the gap diagram around them is authored for this video and is labelled 'CONSTRUCTED ILLUSTRATION' on screen for its full duration.
metadata.claude_response_disclosure: No Claude chat transcript or generated conversational response appears on screen. The composer beats (B00, B08) show a prompt being TYPED, not a claimed Claude answer; B00's output lines are the three findings this video itself demonstrates, not a transcript.

beats.narration_text: Nine percent, twenty-four and a half percent, sixty-six and a half percent. Those are real numbers from the course code. Sample that distribution a thousand times and the favourite should come up six hundred sixty-five times. It came up six hundred thirty. This is Liam, in for Bear.
beats.new_visual_element: Cold open — the composer asks the question the reel answers

show.event: Cream Claude composer, serif greeting 'Namaste, Liam' above the card
The ask types itself into the composer, character by character
Send button arms terracotta; runningText 'running main.py…' appears
Three result lines land in sequence beneath the composer

props.command: main.py says index 2 has probability 0.6652. Over 1000 draws that predicts 665.24 hits. The run returned 630. Is the probability wrong?
output: one run of 1000 cannot settle it

beats.narration_text: Run it a thousand times. The math says six sixty-five. You get six hundred thirty. A gap that size is unusual — about one run in fifty. But unusual is not the same as wrong.
beats.new_visual_element: Hesitant-writer executive summary; the misconception is typed, then corrected

show.event: Empty cream page; 0.8s of silence before the first character (lead_silence_s)
Writer types the first three lines, hesitating mid-phrase
Types 'That looks broken.' — the word 'broken' renders in terracotta: it is doomed
Long pause. The writer deletes 'broken' character by character
Types 'normal' in its place. The corrected sentence holds to the cut

props.text:
Run it a thousand times.
The math says 665.
You get 630.
That gap is proof.

beats.authoring_note: CORRECTION = the reel's actual misconception, per EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW. Single-word trigger is FORCED, not a style choice: BrutalistHesitantWriter.tsx:133 matches triggers against single whitespace-delimited tokens (triggers.indexOf(core.toLowerCase())), so a multi-word phrase can never match — see FRICTIONAL.md 2026-09-26. 'broken' -> 'normal' flips the whole sentence, which is what the law actually asks for.

beats.narration_text: Where does sixty-six and a half percent come from? Three raw scores — one, two, three — go into softmax. Subtract the largest, exponentiate, divide by the total. Out comes zero point six six five two. That is the only thing this video borrows from softmax.
beats.new_visual_element: SoftmaxInOneBeat — three logits become three probabilities, in one pass

show.event: Row 1: the three logits 1, 2, 3 land as mono chips
Row 2: each chip slides down and re-labels to -2, -1, 0 (peak subtracted)
Row 3: values become 0.1353, 0.3679, 1.0000 — the exponentials
A divisor bar draws under the row with the real sum 1.5032
Row 4 resolves to 0.0900, 0.2447, 0.6652; only 0.6652 takes terracotta
Footer chip: 'this reel uses ONE of these numbers'

beats.authoring_note: SCOPE GUARD. This beat sources one number and explicitly hands off. The max-subtraction is a different listed concept and is NOT taught here. All four rows are real: exp(-2)=0.13533, exp(-1)=0.36788, exp(0)=1.0, sum=1.50321.

beats.narration_text: Expected count is one multiplication. Zero point six six five two, times a thousand draws, is six hundred sixty-five point two four. That is not a prediction about any single run. It is the long-run average, if you repeated the whole thousand-draw experiment over and over.
beats.new_visual_element: ExpectedCount — the multiplication performs itself, then is bounded

show.event: 0.6652409557748218 types across the frame at full printed precision
'x 1000' swings in beneath it; the multiplication rule draws
A counter spins up from 0 and settles on 665.24 in terracotta
Caption strikes through 'what this run will do'
and replaces it with 'the average over many runs' — the bound, on the spoken word

beats.narration_text: Here is what actually ran. Seed seven, a thousand draws, straight from main dot py. Index zero: one hundred and two. Index one: two hundred and sixty-eight. Index two, the favourite: six hundred and thirty. Not six sixty-five. Six hundred and thirty.
beats.new_visual_element: ObservedCounts — the real Counter output, bars growing to their true values

show.event: The verbatim JSON block from main.py fades in at left, key order 1/2/0 as printed
Three bars build at right, each growing as its count is spoken
Bar 0 grows to 102
Bar 1 grows to 268
Bar 2 grows to 630 and takes terracotta
A dashed rule drops at 665.24 — the bar visibly stops short of it

beats.authoring_note: The JSON block reproduces the printed key order (1, 2, 0) rather than sorting it — see FRICTIONAL.md. Bars are drawn in index order and labelled, so the reordering is visible rather than silently tidied.

beats.narration_text: Thirty-five point two four draws short. About five percent below the expected count. In sampling terms that is two point four standard deviations — roughly a one in fifty result. Fair warning: this picture is built for the video. The two numbers are real. The shape around them is mine.
beats.new_visual_element: TheGap — the 35.24 difference, explicitly labelled as a constructed illustration

show.event: 'CONSTRUCTED ILLUSTRATION' chip is present from frame 1 and never leaves
A number line draws; 630 and 665.24 land as two marks
The span between them fills terracotta; '35.24' counts up over it
'≈ 5.3% below expected' resolves under the span
Footnote types: 'numbers real · diagram authored for this video'

beats.authoring_note: ASSIGNMENT REQUIREMENT: 'Label constructed illustrations as constructed.' The chip is on screen for the beat's full duration, not flashed. 35.24 = 665.2409557748218 - 630; 35.24/665.24 = 5.297%.

beats.narration_text: So does that settle it? No — but not because the gap is ordinary. It is not. Only about one run in fifty lands this low. It settles nothing because this is a single draw, from one fixed seed, looked at after the fact. A one in fifty result is a reason to test, not a verdict. What would settle it is repetition — many runs, and a check on where six hundred thirty really falls.
beats.new_visual_element: WhatWouldSettleIt — one run versus many runs, and where the evidence actually lives

show.event: Left panel: a single tick at 630 — one lonely observation
'Can this refute 0.6652?' resolves beneath it, then stamps NO
Right panel: ticks accumulate into a spread centred near 665
The 630 tick re-appears inside that spread, unremarkable
The right panel dims to ~45% and a terracotta rule labels it 'NOT RUN IN THIS VIDEO'

beats.authoring_note: Right panel is a SCHEMATIC of an experiment not performed — it is dimmed and captioned as such, so it can never read as data I collected. Legibility contract: dimmed panel stays at 45%, above the 40% floor.

beats.narration_text: The honest verdict. Expected count is what the math predicts. Observed count is what happened once. Six hundred thirty is genuinely low — about one in fifty. And a seed makes that run repeatable, not correct. What this video does not establish is that zero point six six five two is wrong. One seeded run, read after the fact, cannot show that.
beats.new_visual_element: Verdict artifact page — the four claims, and the named boundary

show.event: Claude window opens on the artifact view, titled 'Expected, Observed'
Line 1 lands: expected = what the math predicts
Line 2: observed = what happened once
Line 3: a seed buys repeatability, not correctness
Line 4 lands in terracotta — the boundary this video does NOT cross

props.artifactHeading: What this does and does not establish
artifactLines: Expected count 665.24 — what the math predicts.
630 is ~2.4 sd below expected: about 1 run in 50.
NOT ESTABLISHED: that 0.6652 is wrong — one run cannot show it.

beats.authoring_note: ASSIGNMENT REQUIREMENT (2 pts): 'Name one thing your explanation does not establish.' Stated plainly, in terracotta, unhedged.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: run the lesson one sampler a hundred times, with a hundred different seeds, a thousand draws each. Plot how often index two comes up, and mark where six hundred and thirty falls. I calculated that it should land in the tail, about one run in fifty. But that is arithmetic, not a measurement. A hundred runs turn it into one. And if the plot disagrees with my number, the plot is right.
